PASSO 1: o objeto direto é quem recebe a: STEP 1: the direct object is whoever receives the action of the verb: «Veo la casa», «Veo a Ana». When that object is a specific person, Spanish puts «a» before it: «Veo a Ana» (I see Ana), «Llamo a mi hermano» (I'm calling my brother). This is the personal «a», and English has nothing like it — it isn't translated. STEP 2: the personal «a» is also used for a pet with a name or one you love («Quiero mucho a mi gato»), and with «alguien», «nadie» and «quién» («No veo a nadie», «¿A quién esperas?» — Who are you waiting for?). STEP 3: it isn't used after «tener», or after «hay» to say what there is: «Tengo dos hermanos», «Hay muchos estudiantes». STEP 4: it isn't used with things: «Busco un hotel», not «busco a un hotel». STEP 5: with an unspecified person (anyone at all), the «a» disappears: «Busco un médico que hable alemán»; with a specific person, it comes back: «Busco al médico de mi madre». STEP 6: the direct object pronouns are «lo» (him, it), «la» (her, it), «los» and «las»; the indirect object pronouns are «le» (to him, to her, to you-usted) and «les». «Lo vi» = I saw him (Pablo); «Le di el libro» = I gave him/her the book. STEP 7: CAUTION, leísmo: in Spain many people say «le» instead of «lo» when the direct object is a man: «Le vi ayer» instead of «Lo vi ayer». The standard accepts this only for a single male person. In Latin America «lo» dominates. STEP 8: laísmo («La dije la verdad») and loísmo («Lo di un libro») are considered incorrect: what you give or say to someone is an indirect object, so the pronoun is «le», whether it's a man or a woman: «Le dije la verdad», «Le di un libro». STEP 9: as a learner, use «lo» and «la» for direct objects and «le» for indirect objects; recognise leísmo when you hear it, without needing to adopt it.
em português escrevemos «vejo a Ana» e «: English "I see Ana" and "I'm calling my brother" have no preposition, but Spanish requires «a» before a specific person: «veo a Ana», «llamo a mi hermano». And English "him/her" doesn't tell you direct from indirect, but Spanish does: «lo/la» (direct) vs «le» (indirect): «La veo» (I see her) × «Le digo la verdad» (I tell her the truth).

PASSO 1: em espanhol, muitos verbos pede: STEP 1: many Spanish verbs take a fixed preposition, and it's often not the English one. The best approach is to learn the verb and its preposition as one block. STEP 2: some differ from English: «pensar en» (think about), «soñar con» (dream of), «casarse con» (marry, literally "marry with"), «enamorarse de» (fall in love with), «depender de» (depend on), «contar con» (count on), «acordarse de» (remember). STEP 3: others take «a» before an infinitive: «empezar a», «aprender a», «ayudar a», «volver a» (to do again): «Vuelvo a llamar mañana» (I'll call again tomorrow). Those with «de»: «dejar de» (stop doing), «acabar de» (have just done), «tratar de» (try to). And «tardar en» (take a long time to), «insistir en», «consistir en», «fijarse en» (notice). STEP 4: several verbs that take a preposition in English take none in Spanish: «buscar trabajo» (look FOR work), «pedir ayuda» (ask FOR help), «esperar el autobús» (wait FOR the bus), «mirar la tele» (look AT the TV), «escuchar la radio» (listen TO the radio). STEP 5: if a «que» clause follows the verb, keep the preposition when the verb requires it: «Me di cuenta de que era tarde» (I realised it was late), «Estoy seguro de que viene», «Depende de que llueva» (with subjunctive). Dropping that «de» is called queísmo, and careful speakers avoid it. STEP 6: the opposite is also a mistake: don't add «de» where the verb doesn't want it: «Creo que vienes», not «creo de que vienes» (dequeísmo). STEP 7: review of «por» and «para» (lesson 31). «Por» expresses cause («Gracias por tu ayuda»), exchange («Pago diez euros por el libro»), route and vague location («Viajo por Sudamérica»), part of the day («por la mañana»), duration («por un año») and agent («escrito por mi hermana»). «Para» expresses purpose («Estudio para aprobar»), recipient («Es para ti»), deadline («Lo necesito para el lunes»), destination («Salgo para Madrid») and opinion («Para mí, es fácil»). STEP 8: trick: if you can swap it for "because of" or "in exchange for", it's «por»; if you can swap it for "in order to" or "towards", it's «para».
em português dizemos «sonhar com», «pens: English phrasal prepositions are the trap: "look FOR" = «buscar», "wait FOR" = «esperar», "ask FOR" = «pedir», "listen TO" = «escuchar» — no preposition in Spanish. Meanwhile "dream OF" = «soñar CON», "think ABOUT" = «pensar EN», "marry" = «casarse CON». And English "thanks FOR" is «gracias POR», never «para»; "it's FOR you" is «es PARA ti».

PASSO 1: lembre da ordem (aulas 23 a 25): STEP 1: remember the order (lessons 23 to 25): the indirect object pronoun comes before the direct one: «me lo», «te la», «se lo». When «le» or «les» comes before «lo, la, los, las», it changes to «se»: «Se lo doy» (I give it to him). STEP 2: with an infinitive, the pronoun can go before the conjugated verb or be attached to the infinitive: «Lo quiero comprar» = «Quiero comprarlo». With «ir a»: «Te lo voy a decir» = «Voy a decírtelo». STEP 3: the same with the gerund: «Lo estoy leyendo» = «Estoy leyéndolo». When the pronoun is attached, a written accent appears to keep the stress on the same syllable: «leyéndolo», «diciéndomelo». STEP 4: with an affirmative command, the pronoun is always attached: «Cómpralo» (Buy it), «Dímelo» (Tell me), «Dáselo». When two pronouns are attached, or the verb is long, there's almost always a written accent. STEP 5: with a negative command, the pronoun goes before the verb: «No lo compres», «No me lo digas». STEP 6: with affirmative «vosotros», the final «-d» drops before «os»: «sentaos», «levantaos» (exception: «idos»). STEP 7: the pronoun never sits in the middle of a verb sequence: not «puedes me explicar», but «puedes explicarme» or «me puedes explicar».
em português o pronome pode vir antes ou: English pronouns always come after the verb: "buy it", "tell me". In Spanish they come BEFORE a conjugated verb («lo compro»), and are attached AFTER infinitives, gerunds and affirmative commands, written as one word: «comprarlo», «dímelo». The written accent shows the verb keeps its original stressed syllable.

Una mudanza con amigos / Uma mudança com: Una mudanza con amigos / Moving house with friends
No sábado Inés se mudou para um apartame: On Saturday Inés moved into a new flat and her friends helped her. Pablo brought the van and wouldn't let anyone else have it: "I'm driving it," he said. Carlos was putting the books into boxes. When Inés asked him if he'd counted them, he replied: "I'm counting them now." To carry the sofa upstairs, Inés told the others: "Don't lift it on your own; wait for me and I'll help you." Later, seeing that the lamp was broken, Inés called her sister: "Buy me one the same, please, and bring it tomorrow." Her sister replied: "I'll buy it today and bring it over." In the end, everyone sat on the floor and ate pizza. Inés said: "Thank you, everyone. Sit down and eat, you've earned it."
